\chapter{Please}
\label{ch:te-please}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say please in Telugu, and use the polite -aṇḍi verb ending speakers actually reach for.}

Build \te{దయచేసి} out of daya (\textquotedblleft{}compassion\textquotedblright{}) + cēsi (\textquotedblleft{}having done\textquotedblright{}), then make the everyday polite request instead: \te{కూర్చోండి}, \textquotedblleft{}please sit.\textquotedblright{}
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dayacēsi]{\te{దయచేసి} (dayacēsi) — please (having done compassion)}

\label{lesson:TE-C08-dayachesi}



\begin{quote}
Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} carries a whole small sentence inside it: \textquotedblleft{}having \textbf{done} (me) a compassion.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} = \textbf{please}, literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done kindness / compassion}.\textquotedblright{} Two pieces:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{దయ}} (\emph{daya}) = \textbf{compassion, kindness, grace} — from Sanskrit \textbf{daya}.
  \item \textbf{\te{చేసి}} (\emph{cēsi}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done},\textquotedblright{} from the verb \textbf{\te{చేయు}} (\emph{cēyu}) \textquotedblleft{}to do.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{dayacēsi} is \emph{having done (a) kindness} — you ask by crediting the listener with the grace you hope they'll show.

It is the twin of \textbf{Tamil} \emph{tayavu seytu} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{do} the kindness\textquotedblright{}) — both use a \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} verb — and cousins with \textbf{Kannada} \emph{dayaviṭṭu} (\textquotedblleft{}having \textbf{placed} compassion\textquotedblright{}). Further off, \textbf{Arabic} \emph{min faḍlik} (\textquotedblleft{}from your \textbf{grace}\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{Hindi} \emph{kṛpayā} (from \emph{kṛpā}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{compassion}\textquotedblright{}) ask in the very same spirit.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{daya} + a light verb, four ways:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} \emph{daya\textbf{cēsi}} — compassion \textbf{+ having done}
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{தயவுசெய்து}} \emph{tayavu \textbf{sey}tu} — kindness \textbf{+ do}
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು}} \emph{daya\textbf{viṭṭu}} — compassion \textbf{+ having placed}
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} \emph{daya\textbf{vāyi}} — compassion \textbf{+ as / having become}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: Sound \& structure point}
The middle syllable \textbf{\te{చే}} is \emph{ca} wearing the \textbf{long‑ē} sign \textbf{‑\te{ే}} (the counterpart of the short‑e sign \textbf{‑\te{ె}}), giving \emph{cē}; then \textbf{\te{సి}} is \emph{sa} + the \emph{i} sign (\textbf{‑\te{ి}}). Telugu marks a vowel's length and quality by the little sign riding on the consonant — the consonant stays put, the vowel-sign changes the tune.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}daya\textquotedblright{} — compassion — then \textquotedblleft{}cēsi,\textquotedblright{} having done
  \item the whole word — \textquotedblleft{}dayacēsi\textquotedblright{} = please
  \item the two pieces again, slowly — \textquotedblleft{}daya\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}cēsi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Telugu word for please? (\textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} \emph{dayacēsi}.) What do its pieces mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Compassion}\textquotedblright{} \emph{daya} + \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having done}\textquotedblright{} \emph{cēsi}.) Which cousins ask the same way? (\textbf{Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam} with \emph{daya} — plus \textbf{Arabic} \emph{faḍl}, \textbf{Hindi} \emph{kṛpā}.) Which sign sits on the middle syllable? (\textbf{The long‑ē sign ‑\te{ే}}, making \te{చ} into \te{చే}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-aṇḍi]{‑\te{ండి} (-aṇḍi) — where Telugu actually keeps \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C08-andi}



\begin{quote}
You now have \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} for \emph{please}. Now the honest part: most of the time, a Telugu speaker asking politely does not say it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The ending does the work}
Telugu politeness rides on the \textbf{respectful command ending ‑\te{ండి}} (\emph{-aṇḍi}). It is not a separate word you add — it is a \textbf{tail on the verb}, and it is already \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{respectful form} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{కూర్చోండి}} \emph{kūrcōṇḍi} & please sit \\
\textbf{\te{చెప్పండి}} \emph{ceppaṇḍi} & please tell me \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Each of these is a verb with \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} on the end, and each is already polite — no extra word required. There is a shorter form of every one of them, used with a friend or a child; you will meet those verbs properly later, so take the ‑\te{ండి} forms as wholes for now. The short form is not rude, it is \emph{close}, and using it with a stranger is the mistake. Leaving out \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} is not.

\begin{culture}
The standalone \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} is \textbf{formal or emphatic}. It is not the everyday \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} — it is the one you reach for to \emph{warm a request further}, on top of an ending that is already polite:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{కూర్చోండి}} — please sit. Complete, polite, ordinary.
  \item \textbf{\te{దయచేసి} \te{కూర్చోండి}} — \emph{do} please sit. Warmer, more insistent, more formal.
\end{itemize}

So the two stack. What they do not do is substitute: \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} in front of the \emph{short} form reads as oddly as \textquotedblleft{}kindly sit down, mate.\textquotedblright{}

English keeps politeness in a word you add; Telugu keeps it in the shape of the verb. A learner hunting for a word to translate \emph{please} will reach for \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} far too often and still sound abrupt — because the abruptness was never in the missing word. It was in the ending.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kūrcōṇḍi\textquotedblright{} — that ending is already \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ceppaṇḍi\textquotedblright{} — please tell me
  \item both words together, warmer — \textquotedblleft{}dayacēsi kūrcōṇḍi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What carries \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} in ordinary Telugu speech? (\textbf{The ending ‑\te{ండి}} \emph{-aṇḍi}, on the verb.) Is \textbf{\te{కూర్చోండి}} already polite without \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}}? (\textbf{Yes} — the ending is the politeness.) When do you add \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}}? (To make a request \textbf{warmer or more formal}, on top of ‑\te{ండి}.) What is wrong with putting \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} in front of the short form? (The \textbf{short} ending undercuts the polite word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ca]{\te{చ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S112-letter-ca}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ూ} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{౯}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{చ}}
\textbf{\te{చ}} — \emph{ca}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{c}, it is \textbf{ca}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{చ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{పని} \te{చేయు}} \emph{pani cēyu} — to work (lit. \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుగు} \te{వచ్చు}} \emph{nāku telugu vaccu} — 'I know Telugu'
  \item \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} \emph{dayacēsi} — please (dayacēsi
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{చ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{చ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{చ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{దయచేసి}  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{చ} three times, saying \emph{ca} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{చ} once more
\end{itemize}
